reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / ACR-EULAR
clinicalPearls: An ANCA-associated small-vessel vasculitis with a classic triad of upper airway, lung, and kidney involvement
Upper respiratory features include persistent sinusitis, nasal crusting and bleeding, saddle-nose deformity, and subglottic stenosis
Pulmonary disease ranges from nodules and cavities to life-threatening alveolar haemorrhage
Renal involvement is a pauci-immune, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with an active urinary sediment
Most patients are positive for c-ANCA directed against proteinase 3 (anti-PR3)
Biopsy shows necrotising granulomatous inflammation with vasculitis; renal biopsy shows crescentic glomerulonephritis with little immune deposition
The pulmonary-renal syndrome (diffuse alveolar haemorrhage with glomerulonephritis) is a medical emergency
Treatment has induction and maintenance phases using glucocorticoids combined with rituximab or cyclophosphamide, and plasma exchange is considered in severe organ-threatening disease
reference.pathophysiology: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotising vasculitis of small vessels associated with anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, predominantly against proteinase 3. ANCA activate primed neutrophils, causing degranulation, release of reactive oxygen species and proteases, and endothelial injury, producing pauci-immune (minimal immune complex) inflammation. The disease combines this small-vessel vasculitis with granuloma formation in the respiratory tract. Injury to alveolar capillaries causes diffuse alveolar haemorrhage, and glomerular capillary damage produces crescentic, rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis.
additionalDifferentials: Microscopic polyangiitis and eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis
Chronic infective sinusitis or invasive fungal disease
Malignancy of the upper airway or lung
additionalInvestigations: ANCA testing with PR3 and MPO antigen specificity
Urinalysis and microscopy for dysmorphic red cells and casts, with renal function monitoring
Chest imaging (radiograph and CT) for nodules, cavities, and haemorrhage
Tissue biopsy (renal, lung, or ENT) for necrotising granulomatous vasculitis
Assessment of upper airway including nasendoscopy and evaluation for subglottic stenosis
redFlags: Diffuse alveolar haemorrhage presenting with haemoptysis, hypoxia, and falling haemoglobin
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis with rising creatinine requiring urgent immunosuppression and possible plasma exchange
Airway compromise from subglottic or tracheal stenosis
Ocular involvement such as orbital pseudotumour or scleritis threatening vision
Mononeuritis multiplex or central nervous system involvement
reference.prognosis: Once almost uniformly fatal, the disease now has good remission rates with modern induction therapy, but relapse is common and requires ongoing surveillance. Prognosis is worse with severe renal impairment at presentation and with alveolar haemorrhage; long-term morbidity includes chronic kidney disease and treatment-related complications.
pitfalls: Treating recurrent sinusitis or nasal symptoms as isolated ENT disease and missing systemic vasculitis
Delaying immunosuppression in rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis, risking irreversible renal failure
Assuming a negative ANCA excludes the diagnosis, especially in limited disease
Overlooking early alveolar haemorrhage when haemoptysis is minimal
Failing to monitor for relapse and treatment-related infection during maintenance
management: Induce remission with high-dose glucocorticoids combined with either rituximab or cyclophosphamide for organ-threatening disease
Use the C5a receptor antagonist avacopan as a glucocorticoid-sparing adjunct to reduce steroid exposure
Add plasma exchange in selected patients with severe rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis or diffuse alveolar haemorrhage
Maintain remission with rituximab, azathioprine or methotrexate while tapering glucocorticoids
Provide supportive care with Pneumocystis jirovecii prophylaxis using co-trimoxazole, bone protection and vaccination and infection surveillance
Support acute organ failure, with respiratory support for alveolar haemorrhage and renal replacement therapy for advanced renal failure
Monitor renal function, urinary sediment and ANCA titres for relapse, which is common
Coordinate rheumatology, nephrology, respiratory and ENT input, including management of subglottic stenosis
